entries.one_line: Hear, find, and use notes by the role they play in a key.

intro.text: Every note has a relationship to the
— the home note of a key. Scale-degree recognition helps you hear, locate, and choose those relationships on purpose.

modules.title: Hear the tonal home
modules.explanation: Settle on C as home. Compare C (1), E (3), and G (5) against that tonal center.
steps: Play or sustain C as a reference.
Sing C, E and G, naming their scale degrees.
Return to C after each note and listen for the feeling of home.

modules.title: Name degrees in different keys
modules.explanation: A note's scale degree depends on the key. E is degree 3 in C major and degree 6 in G major.
steps: Write the C major scale and number each note.
Write the G major scale and number its notes.
Compare how E changes its role.

modules.title: Target degrees while improvising
modules.explanation: Navigate to chosen scale degrees in multiple positions without depending on one memorized pattern.
steps: Choose a tonal center and a limited string set.
Locate degrees 3 and 7 in several positions.
Create short phrases that approach each target note.

entries.one_line: Build three-note chords from their root, third, and fifth.

intro.text: contains a root, a third, and a fifth. Changing the third changes a major chord to a minor chord while the root and perfect fifth remain.

modules.title: Spell a major and minor triad
modules.explanation: C major is C–E–G. C minor is C–E♭–G: the third moves down one semitone.
steps: Write C–E–G as root, third and fifth.
Lower E to E♭ and listen for the change.
Try the same comparison with G major and minor.

modules.title: Find three inversions
modules.explanation: The same chord tones can appear in different orders. Verify each note and fingering against the actual tuning.
steps: Spell a three-note chord before choosing fret positions.
Find a root-position voicing on three adjacent strings.
Reorder the same notes into first and second inversion.

modules.title: Connect chords smoothly
modules.explanation: Use voice leading to connect voicings with small movements while keeping each chord's notes correct.
steps: Choose a three-chord progression.
Write several nearby voicings for each chord.
Compare which voices move least between chords.

entries.one_line: Feel the space between beats and choose when notes land.

intro.text: is the pulse you can tap.
divides that pulse into smaller, evenly spaced parts.

modules.title: Keep a steady pulse
modules.explanation: Count 1, 2, 3, 4 over four steady quarter-note beats. Adding 'and' between counts doubles the events without changing the underlying beat.
steps: Tap four equally spaced quarter-note beats.
Keep tapping while saying 1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and.
Stop saying 'and' without changing your tapping speed.

modules.title: Switch between subdivisions
modules.explanation: Alternate quarter notes, eighth notes and sixteenths while keeping the same tempo.
steps: Play one note on each beat for one bar.
Play two even notes per beat for one bar.
Play four even notes per beat for one bar.

modules.title: Shape accents independently
modules.explanation: Make an accent pattern move against a steady pulse without accidentally changing tempo or meter.
steps: Choose a consistent beat and subdivision.
Accent every third subdivision without moving the beat.
Return to a simple accent pattern to test pulse stability.

terms.definition: The home note of a key, heard as a point of arrival or rest.
terms.detail: In C major, C is the tonic. A passage can change its tonal center; the tonic depends on musical context.

terms.definition: A steady pulse that helps organize music in time.
terms.detail: A beat can be divided into smaller parts without changing the tempo.

terms.definition: Dividing one beat into smaller equal time units.
terms.detail: Straight eighth notes place two events in a quarter-note beat; triplets place three.

terms.definition: A chord built from three different pitch classes, commonly stacked in thirds.
terms.detail: Major and minor triads are often described by their root, third and fifth.

terms.definition: The position of a note within a scale, counted from its first degree.
terms.detail: The tonic is scale degree 1. In C major, E is degree 3.

terms.definition: The pitch a chord is named after and built around.
terms.detail: The root of C major is C, even when another chord tone is the lowest note.
Intervals can be described by numbered sizes and qualities, such as major third.
